chunks: MOSFET body diode: origin and effects. The question: What is the internal body diode? Where does it come from?
The body diode is a diode, a one-way valve for current, that exists inside every MOSFET because of how it is built.
It sits between the body (the silicon the channel is built in) and the drain.
In a typical power N-channel MOSFET it points from source to drain, so even with the gate off, current can flow backward through it.
It matters because it can waste power or save you, depending on the circuit.
Imagine a one-way flap built into the wall of a pipe. The main valve is the MOSFET channel, and it can open or close.
But the flap lets water slip backward whenever the pressure is reversed, whatever the valve is doing. You did not add the flap. It came from the way the pipe was made.
A simplified planar cell. The p-body (red) meets the n⁻ drift region (blue) along the green lines: that PN junction is the body diode.
Because the source metal contacts both the n⁺ source and the p-body, the junction sits between source (anode) and drain (cathode).
When the gate is high, a channel forms at the p-body surface under the gate (purple), linking the n⁺ source to the drift region, and electrons then flow down to the drain.
Not to scale.
Body diode: the PN junction between body and drain. Anode / cathode: the two ends of a diode. Current flows easily from anode to cathode.
Freewheeling: letting an inductor's current keep flowing through a path when the switch opens. An inductor is a coil that resists any sudden change in its current.
Dead time: a short gap when both switches in a half-bridge (two switches stacked between supply and ground) are off.
Synchronous rectification: turning the channel on so current avoids the diode's 0. 7 volts drop.
Take an NMOS with its source on ground and its gate at 0 volts, so it is off. Now let the circuit pull current out of the drain, trying to drag it below ground.
The body diode turns on, current flows from source to drain, and the drain stops about 0. 7 volts below ground, even though the gate says off.
With 2 amps through it, that is about 2 times 0. 7 equals 1. 4 watts of heat. That is the whole idea.
"The body diode is the PN junction between the MOSFET's body and its drain, there because of how the transistor is built.
With the body tied to the source, an NMOS has a diode with its anode at the source and cathode at the drain, so the FET can't block voltage in the reverse direction, and a PMOS is the opposite.
It matters in half-bridges: during dead time inductor current flows through it at 0.
7 to 1 volts and it has reverse-recovery charge, so we turn the channel on for synchronous rectification, and use back-to-back FETs when we need two-way blocking."
